newsitem.title: USA: U.S. clears Jewell of Atlanta Olympic bombing.
newsitem.headline: U.S. clears Jewell of Atlanta Olympic bombing.

text.p: The U.S. Justice Department on Saturday officially cleared Richard Jewell of being a suspect in its investigation into the Olympic park bombing.

Nearly three months after the former Olympic security guard became the only named suspect in the probe, the U.S. Attorney Kent Alexander issued a letter to Jewell's criminal defence lawyer saying his client was no longer being targeted by the FBI.
Alexander also said in the letter that he hopes Jewell now will cooperate with the investigation as a witness.

"This is to advise you that based on the evidence developed to date, your client Richard Jewell is not considered a target of the federal criminal investigation into the bombing on July 27, 1996, at Centennial Olympic Park in Atlanta," the federal prosecutor wrote.
"Barring any newly discovered evidence, this status will not change."
The letter did not include the apology sought by Jewell and his family for the FBI's handling of the investigation, which Jewell claims has ruined his chances of getting another job.

But in a separate statement to the media, the U.S. Attorney noted that Jewell and his mother, Barbara, had "regretably also endured highly unusual and intense publicity that was neither designed nor desired by the FBI and, in fact, interfered with the investigation."
Jack Martin, the attorney to whom Alexander addressed the letter, was not immediately available for comment. Jewell and his lawyers were expected to appear at a news conference on Monday.
The letter was a long sought vindication for Jewell, who steadfastly maintained his innocence throughout weeks of FBI surveillance and round-the-clock media scrutiny.

The July 27 bombing came midway through the Atlanta Olympic Games. A pipe bomb hidden in a green knapsack exploded during a free concert in downtown Atlanta, leaving two people dead and more than 100 wounded.

The 33-year-old Jewell was initially hailed as a hero in the case. While working as a security guard at a nearby AT&T pavillion, he noticed the suspicious knapsack, alerted police and helped clear concert-goers from the area before the bomb detonated.
Three days later, however, he fell under the glare of international publicity when an unsourced newspaper article identified him as a suspect.
Jewell hired a team of four attorneys to defend him against the investigation and to explore the potential grounds for lawsuits against both the government and members of the news media.
In the meanwhile, his mother made a tearful public appeal in which she asked President Bill Clinton to clear her son.
Signs that Jewell's role as a suspect had begun to diminish surfaced earlier this month when FBI agents abandoned their stakeout of his family's suburban Atlanta apartment.
Jewell agreed to submit to a six-hour interrogation on Oct. 6, with the understanding that a letter clearing him of suspicion would be issued if investigators were satisfied with his statements.

Earlier this week, a federal judge in Atlanta also ordered the public disclosure of sealed affidavits used to obtain federal search warrants against Jewell, saying former guard no longer appeared to be a suspect in the case.
